theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: For a clinic in Savanna-la-Mar, the drawing and the specification give different conduit sizes for one run. Who should settle it?
options: The trainee who will install that run
The supplier, who knows which size is in stock
The designer, through a written query
Whoever gets to the site first that morning

questions.stem: Why does a Level 3 electrician read the whole specification, not only the drawings, before preparing a job?
options: The drawings are only there for the customer to see
The specification lists the pay rates for the team
The specification is shorter and quicker to read
It sets materials, methods and tests not drawn

questions.stem: A workshop owner in Portmore expects to add and move machines often. Which wiring system suits the main runs best?
options: Conduit cast into the concrete floor
Cable tray or trunking with spare room
Cables clipped straight onto the walls
Flexible cords run across the floor

questions.stem: In a hotel lobby, no wiring may be seen once the job is finished. Which approach is best?
options: Surface PVC conduit painted the same colour as the walls
Surface trunking fixed high up near the ceiling line
Cables clipped neatly along the top of the skirting
Concealed conduit, fixed before walls and ceilings are finished

questions.stem: Conduit must be cast into a concrete roof slab that will be poured next week. What must happen before the pour?
options: Fix and cap the conduit and boxes, then have it checked
Nothing, as the conduit can be fixed after the pour is done
Lay the conduit loose on the steel so it can move as needed
Ask the builder to cut channels once the concrete has set

questions.stem: Why should sleeves and openings for cable routes be agreed with the builder before walls and floors are built?
options: Builders do not allow electricians to drill at all
Sleeves cost less when the builder buys them in bulk
Late holes cost more and can weaken the structure
The inspector only passes sleeves fitted in advance

questions.stem: Your first fix in one wing depends on the ceiling grid, which is a week late. What should you do?
options: Wait in that wing until the ceiling grid is finished
Tell your supervisor and re-plan other areas first
Fix the conduit there now and move it again later
Send the team home until the builder is ready again

questions.stem: A 1320 W pump runs on 110 V. What current does it draw?
options: 6 A

questions.stem: Each heater on a 110 V circuit takes 1200 W. The circuit is protected at 30 A. How many heaters can run at the same time?
A cable's voltage drop is 18 mV per amp per metre. It will carry 20 A over a 25 m route. What is the voltage drop?
options: 9 V

questions.stem: For a long 220 V run, the smaller of two cable sizes passes the current rating but fails the voltage drop limit. Which should you choose?
options: The smaller one, since it carries the current
The smaller one, with a bigger breaker fitted
Either one, as voltage drop is not a safety matter
The larger one, since both checks must pass

questions.stem: Why may a cable need to be larger when it runs through a hot roof space?
options: Hot air makes the copper heavier per metre
Heat around it lowers the current it can safely carry
Hot roof spaces need an extra earth conductor
Larger cables are easier to pull in hot air

questions.stem: Why does bunching many circuits together in one conduit affect the cable size you choose?
options: Bunched cables carry a higher voltage
Each cable must then carry the others' load
Bunched cables cannot lose heat so easily
Bunched cables need thicker colour coding

questions.stem: A trainee picks a cable size from the breaker rating alone. What has he left out?
options: Length, voltage drop and how the cable is run
The colour of the cable's outer sheath on site
The name of the supplier and the drum number
The number of outlets the customer may add one day

questions.stem: Before adding circuits to an existing board in a guest house in Ocho Rios, what should you check?
options: Only that the board door opens and closes freely
Spare ways, condition, earthing and capacity
Only the colour of the board and its cover screws
That it is the same brand as the new breakers

questions.stem: During the survey you find the existing board has no main earth connection. What should you do?
options: Carry on, since the new circuits will have earths
Join the earth bar to the nearest water pipe
Note it on the take-off and deal with it at the end
Report it in writing as a danger before going on

questions.stem: The job needs the whole building's supply off for two hours. What should the plan include?
options: An agreed time, notice to occupants, and lock-off
Switching off without any warning, to save time
Working live so the building keeps its power on
Switching off at night, when no one needs asking

questions.stem: Two electricians and a trainee will work on one isolated circuit. How should the isolator be locked off?
options: The leader's lock alone, as he is in charge of the job
Each person's own lock on a multi-lock hasp
No lock, as all three of them can see the switch
Tape over the switch with a written warning on it

questions.stem: The main switch of a board is off and locked. Why must the incoming terminals still be treated as live?
options: They hold a charge for a few minutes after
They pick up voltage from the earth bar
They are on the supply side of the switch
Locks do not always hold a switch in the off position

questions.stem: A trainee wants to prove a circuit dead with a neon test screwdriver. Why is that wrong?
options: It is not a reliable test between all conductors
It only works on circuits that run at 220 V or more
It can only be used by a qualified inspector
It will blow the fuse in the circuit under test

questions.stem: When is a permit to work most likely to be needed for your preparation work?
options: When you mark out a route on a training bay at the Centre
When you buy the materials from a new supplier
When you work during normal working hours
When the client controls the system's isolation

questions.stem: Your team will work in a roof space in Clarendon in July. Which control matters most for heat stress?
options: Working through lunch so the job is done sooner
Wearing extra layers to keep the sun off the skin
Short spells, water breaks, air flow, buddy checks
Drinking water only at the end of each working day

questions.stem: Why is a mobile tower usually better than a ladder for fixing a long run of conduit along a ceiling?
options: A tower can be put up by one person in a minute
It gives a stable platform with both hands free
Towers do not need to be checked before use
A ladder cannot reach higher than 2 m

questions.stem: A ladder must reach 4 m up a wall. Using the 1-out-for-every-4-up rule, how far from the wall should its foot be?
options: 2 m
4 m
1 m

questions.stem: Who should see the risk assessment for the job before work begins?
options: Everyone doing the work, who signs to say they understood
Only the customer who is paying for the job
Only the team leader, who keeps it in the van
Only the safety officer at the head office

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a risk assessment and a method statement?
options: One is for the customer; the other is for the supplier
One is written after the job; the other before it
One finds hazards; the other sets out safe steps
One lists the tools; the other lists the materials

questions.stem: Why check the calibration date on the continuity and insulation tester before a job starts?
options: Older testers are heavier to carry on site
The date shows when the batteries were changed
Customers ask to see the date on every tool
An out-of-date tester may give wrong readings

questions.stem: Why should materials be checked against the schedule when they are delivered, not when they are needed?
options: Suppliers take nothing back after one day
There is still time to replace wrong items
Checking is quicker while the boxes are new
The driver must sign the schedule before leaving

questions.stem: A supplier offers a cheaper conduit that is not the type in the specification. What should you do?
options: Buy it, since all conduit is much the same
Use it only where the customer cannot see it
Get written approval from the designer first
Mix it in with the specified conduit to save money

questions.stem: Steel conduit must be on site by 10 March 2026. The supplier needs 3 weeks. By which date must you order?
options: 17 February
24 February
3 March
10 February

questions.stem: A cable route measures 135 mm on a 1:50 plan, and 1.5 m more is needed to rise to the board. What length of cable is needed?
Copper cable is often stolen from building sites. How should it be kept?
options: Behind the site hut, under a tarpaulin
In the open, so everyone can keep an eye on it
In the back of the team leader's own car
In a locked store, with every drum logged in and out

questions.stem: Why are PVC conduit and fittings kept out of direct sun while stored on site?
options: Sun can warp the lengths and weaken the plastic
Sun makes the colour codes hard to read on site
Sun makes the conduit too heavy to lift safely
Sun dries out the solvent cement inside the tubes

questions.stem: Why does the team leader check the finished floor level with the builder before box heights are set?
options: The builder must sign off every box position
The floor level decides the colour of the boxes
Heights are set from the finished floor
Box heights are set down from the ceiling instead

questions.stem: Which tool marks a level line round a whole room quickly and accurately?
options: A try square
A laser level
A plumb bob
A steel straight edge

questions.stem: The detector shows nothing, but the drawing shows a water pipe near your drill mark. What should you do?
options: Drill anyway, because the detector is more up to date
Drill slowly so you can stop if you hit the pipe
Drill a little to the side and hope for the best
Move the mark or confirm the pipe route first

questions.stem: A new trainee joins your team halfway through a job. What should you do first?
options: Hand over a drill and let them start
Give a site induction on hazards and rules
Tell them to watch from the van all week
Give them the hardest task as a test

questions.stem: How should you share the preparation tasks in a team of four with different levels of skill?
options: Match tasks to skills; pair new with experienced
Give every task to the most skilled person on site
Let each member pick whatever task they like best
Give the new trainees the riskiest tasks to learn

questions.stem: Why should conduit routes be agreed with the air-conditioning installer?
options: They must approve the size of every cable
They supply the conduit for the whole building
Their ducts and pipes may need the same space
They test all the circuits once the job is done

questions.stem: Why do you agree a storage area and working hours with the building owner before the job?
options: So the owner can count the materials each day
So the owner pays for the storage separately
So the electricians can finish earlier each day
So materials are safe and work disturbs no one

questions.stem: Why is it useful to record existing damage, such as cracked tiles or marked walls, before work starts?
options: It gives the team a list of things to repair for free
It shows the damage was there before you started
It helps the team decide where the conduit should go
It is needed for the customer's electricity bill

questions.stem: Why should the plan list the test instruments that will be needed at the end of the job?
options: So the customer can buy them for the team
So the trainees can practise with them first
So they are booked, in date and on site in time
So the supplier can deliver them with the cable

questions.stem: What should the preparation plan say about the waste from the job?
options: Separate metal, plastic and packaging for disposal
Burn the packaging and the off-cuts on the site
Leave all the waste for the building's own cleaners
Put everything into one skip to save time and money

questions.stem: The job falls in the hurricane season. What should the plan include?
options: Nothing extra, as storms rarely hit in working hours
Working through any storm to keep to the programme
Leaving the materials outside so they are easy to reach
Steps to secure materials and stop work safely in a storm

questions.stem: In a typical Jamaican house, which supply voltages would you expect for the general outlets and the water heater?
options: 220 V for the outlets and 110 V for the heater
110 V for both the outlets and the heater
110 V for the outlets and 220 V for the heater
440 V for the heater and 220 V for the outlets

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A 3300 W load runs on 220 V. What current does it draw, in amps?
A cable's voltage drop is 15 mV per amp per metre. It carries 16 A over 30 m. What is the voltage drop, in volts?
What is the name of the level, given by the builder, from which the heights of switches and outlets are measured?
An outlet box must sit 1.2 m above finished floor level. The bare slab is 50 mm below finished floor level. How high above the slab is the box, in millimetres?
Three 1100 W loads share one 220 V circuit and all run together. What is the total current, in amps?
What is the name of the table that lists every cable on a job, with its size, type, route and the circuit it serves?
What is the name of the document that sets out, step by step, how a job will be done safely?
What is the name of the signed document that lets work start on a system that someone else controls, under set conditions?
What two-word name is given to the stage of fixing conduit, boxes and cables before walls and ceilings are finished?
What name is given to the factor that lowers a cable's current rating when it is bunched with other circuits?
A 2 kW heater runs on 220 V. What current does it draw, in amps, to one decimal place?
What is the name of the clamp-like fitting that lets several workers each put their own padlock on one isolator?
What do the letters RCD stand for, on the device that switches off when current leaks to earth?
What supply voltage is usually used in Jamaica for an electric water heater or stove?
A 220 V circuit may have no more than 4% voltage drop. What is the largest drop allowed, in volts, to one decimal place?

essays.stem: A new small hotel in Negril has a lobby, a commercial kitchen and a plant room. For each area, say which wiring system you would choose (for example concealed conduit, surface conduit, trunking or cable tray) and why.
essays.modelAnswer: In the lobby the wiring must not show, so I would use concealed conduit placed in the walls, slab and ceiling before the finishes, with draw-in boxes where they can be reached later. In the kitchen there is heat, steam, grease and frequent washing, so I would use surface conduit that is easy to clean, such as PVC or galvanised steel with sealed, IP-rated boxes, kept away from hot surfaces and wet areas where possible. I would not use open cable tray there because grease and dirt collect on it. In the plant room there are many large cables and the equipment may change, so I would use cable tray or trunking for the main runs, with conduit or flexible conduit for the final drops to each machine. In every area I would follow the specification and check my choice with the designer.
markingPoints: Lobby: concealed conduit placed before finishes, with access points
Kitchen: easy-clean, sealed surface conduit and IP-rated boxes, away from heat and water
Plant room: tray or trunking for main runs, with conduit or flexible conduit to machines
Gives a reason linked to the conditions for each choice
Follows the specification and checks with the designer

essays.stem: Explain the factors you consider when choosing the cable size for a new 220 V circuit. Include a voltage drop check, with figures.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the design current of the load. For a 3300 W load on 220 V that is 3300 ÷ 220 = 15 A. I choose a protective device of at least that rating, and the cable must carry at least the device rating. The cable's rating depends on how it is installed: if it runs in a hot roof space or is bunched with other circuits, I apply the factors from the tables, so a larger cable may be needed. Then I check voltage drop. If the cable's figure is 18 mV per amp per metre and the run is 25 m, the drop is 18 × 15 × 25 ÷ 1000 = 6.75 V. As a percentage of 220 V that is about 3.1%. If the specification allows 5% (11 V), the cable is acceptable. If it failed, I would choose a larger size or a shorter route. I also check the cable type suits the place it runs.
markingPoints: Works out the design current (I = P ÷ V)
Protective device and cable rating matched to the current
Installation conditions: heat and grouping factors from the tables
Voltage drop worked out correctly and compared with the allowed percentage
Action if it fails (bigger cable or shorter route); cable type suits the location

essays.stem: Your team of three will add circuits to a board that supplies a working guest house in Ocho Rios. Explain how you would plan and carry out safe isolation for the whole team.
essays.modelAnswer: I would agree a time for the outage with the owner and give the guests and staff notice, so fridges, pumps and security systems can be planned for. On the day I would identify the right isolator from the board schedule and switch it off. Each of us would fit our own padlock to a multi-lock hasp, and I would fit a danger tag with my name, the date and the reason. I would check my two-pole voltage tester on a proving unit, then test at the point of work between line and neutral, line and earth, and neutral and earth, then check the tester on the proving unit again. I would warn the team that the incoming supply terminals are still live, and cover them. Only when everyone has removed their own lock, the work is checked and tested, and the area is clear would the supply be restored.
markingPoints: Agrees the time and gives notice to the people affected
Identifies and switches off the correct isolator
Each worker fits their own lock on a hasp; tag with name, date and reason
Proves dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after, between all conductors
Warns about live incoming terminals; restores supply only when all locks are off and work is checked

essays.stem: Explain how you would work with the builder and other trades before and during the first fix in a new two-storey building.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work starts I would go through the drawings with the builder and the other trades, such as plumbing and air conditioning, to agree routes and find clashes. I would ask for sleeves and openings to be placed in walls, beams and floors before they are built, so we do not cut holes later. Where conduit is cast into slabs, I would agree the date of the pour, fix and cap the conduit and boxes in time, and ask for it to be checked before the concrete goes in. I would get the finished floor and ceiling levels from the builder so box heights are right. During the job I would go to site meetings, follow the programme, and tell the builder early if our work will be late or if their work stops ours. Any change of route would be agreed in writing and marked on the drawings.
markingPoints: Reviews drawings with the builder and trades to agree routes and find clashes
Asks for sleeves and openings before walls and floors are built
Fixes and caps cast-in conduit before the pour and has it checked
Gets finished levels for box heights; follows the programme and attends site meetings
Raises delays early; agrees and records any changes

essays.stem: Describe the documents you would prepare before starting a conduit and wiring job, and what each one should contain.
essays.modelAnswer: The risk assessment lists the hazards of the job, such as work at height, existing live circuits, dust, noise, heat and manual handling, who could be harmed, and the controls. The method statement sets out the safe steps in order, including how safe isolation will be done, the access equipment, and who supervises. The materials schedule lists every item with type, size and quantity from the take-off, plus waste allowance, the supplier and the date it must be ordered. The programme, often a bar chart, shows each task, how long it takes, the order and the people needed. Where the client controls the system, a permit to work is arranged. I would also prepare a test plan listing the tests and instruments for the end. The team reads and signs the risk assessment and method statement, and my supervisor approves them.
markingPoints: Risk assessment: hazards, who is at risk, controls
Method statement: safe steps in order, including safe isolation and access
Materials schedule with quantities, suppliers and order dates
Programme or bar chart showing tasks, order, times and people; permit where needed
Team reads and signs; supervisor approves

essays.stem: Before a partial rewire of an old shop in Montego Bay, describe the site survey you would carry out and what you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: I would take the drawings, if any, and walk every room with the owner. At the board I would record its make, size, condition, spare ways and the rating of the main switch, and look for signs of overheating. I would check that a main earth is present and connected, and note the supply voltage arrangement, such as 110 V and 220 V circuits. I would identify which circuits feed which areas, labelling them where the chart is missing, with the power off where I need to open anything. I would note hazards such as damaged cables, possible asbestos, fragile ceilings and access problems, and use a detector to find hidden services along the planned routes. I would measure the routes, note fixing surfaces and existing damage, and take photos. All of this goes into a written survey report, with dangers reported at once.
markingPoints: Board: condition, spare ways, main switch rating, signs of overheating
Earthing present; supply arrangement noted
Identifies circuits safely (isolating before opening anything)
Records hazards and hidden services; measures routes; notes existing damage with photos
Writes a survey report and reports dangers at once

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the ordering, delivery, storage and security of materials for a two-week conduit and wiring job.
essays.modelAnswer: From the take-off I would make a materials schedule with quantities and a waste allowance. I would ask suppliers for lead times and order early enough, counting back from the day each item is needed, especially for special fittings that take weeks. I would plan deliveries in stages so the site is not crowded and items arrive just before they are used. I would agree a delivery point and a dry, lockable store with the owner. On delivery I would check every item against the delivery note and the schedule for type, size, quantity and damage, and report shortages at once. Cable drums would be logged in and out because copper is often stolen. PVC would be kept flat and out of the sun, and steel off the ground. At the end I would return unused stock and record what was used.
markingPoints: Materials schedule from the take-off with a waste allowance
Orders by working back from need dates using lead times
Staged deliveries to a planned point and a secure, dry store
Checks deliveries against the note and the schedule; reports shortages
Security for cable; correct storage of PVC and steel; returns and records

essays.stem: You lead a team of four, including one new trainee, on the preparation stage of a job. Describe how you would brief, organise and supervise them.
essays.modelAnswer: On the first morning I would give a briefing: the scope, the drawings, the programme for the day, the hazards and controls from the risk assessment, emergency points, and who to report to. The new trainee would get a full site induction first. I would share tasks by skill: an experienced member sets out routes with the laser level, another checks deliveries, and I would pair the trainee with an experienced member to mark box positions and learn. I would make sure everyone has the right PPE and tools. During the day I would check work at stages, answer questions and correct mistakes early, explaining why. Safe isolation would be done only by competent members, with every worker's lock on. At the end of the day I would check progress against the plan, record it, and agree the next day's tasks.
markingPoints: Briefing covers scope, programme, hazards, emergencies and reporting
Induction for the new trainee
Tasks matched to skills; trainee paired with an experienced member
Checks work at stages and corrects with explanation; safe isolation by competent members only
End-of-day progress check, record and plan for next day

essays.stem: Explain the hazards of preparing and setting out conduit routes in hot roof spaces and at height in Jamaica, and how you would control them.
essays.modelAnswer: Roof spaces under zinc or concrete roofs can get very hot, which causes heat exhaustion and heat stroke. I would plan that work for the cooler early morning, use short spells with breaks, provide drinking water, use fans where possible, and have workers check on each other. Roof spaces may have fragile ceilings, so workers must stand only on joists or boards laid across them, never on the ceiling. There may be hidden cables, nails, wasps and rats, so we would use good lighting, gloves and long sleeves, and isolate any circuits we must touch. Working at height from ladders and towers risks falls, so access equipment must be checked, set up correctly and used by trained people, with the area below kept clear. Dust from old ceilings needs masks and goggles. Someone outside the roof space should always know who is inside.
markingPoints: Heat stress: timing, breaks, water, air flow, buddy checks
Fragile ceilings: stand only on joists or boards
Hidden cables, sharp objects, pests: lighting, PPE, isolation
Falls from height: checked access equipment, trained users, area below kept clear
Dust controls and someone outside knowing who is in the roof space

essays.stem: A customer has bought machines from overseas for a new workshop. Explain what you would check on their nameplates and why, before planning the circuits.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica's supply is 110 V and 220 V single-phase at 50 Hz, but imported equipment may be made for other voltages or frequencies. I would read each nameplate for the rated voltage, frequency, number of phases, power or current, and any starting current. If a machine needs a voltage or frequency we do not have, it may run badly, overheat or be damaged, so I would report it before any circuit is planned, and the customer may need a different model or a transformer the maker approves. The power or current tells me the circuit current, so I can size the cable and protection and check the board has the capacity. I would also note the IP rating, earthing needs and the maker's installation instructions. All of this goes into the design notes, and anything unclear is checked with the supplier or the designer.
markingPoints: States Jamaica's supply: 110 V and 220 V, single-phase, 50 Hz
Reads voltage, frequency, phases and power or current on the nameplate
Explains the risk of a mismatch and reports it before planning
Uses the current to size cable and protection and to check board capacity
Notes IP rating, earthing and the maker's instructions; checks unclear items with supplier or designer

practical1.title: Survey an installation and prepare the documents for an extension
practical1.brief: The assessor shows the group a training room or bay at the Centre (with its supply isolated and locked off by the assessor) and asks for an extension: three new outlets and two lights in conduit, plus a 220 V circuit for a water heater. As a group: (1) survey the area and the board, and record the board's condition, spare ways, earthing and the existing circuits; (2) mark the new routes and box positions on a copy of the drawing; (3) work out the design current and the voltage drop for the water heater circuit, using the cable data the assessor gives; (4) write the risk assessment and the method statement, including how safe isolation will be done; (5) make the materials schedule with order dates, using lead times the assessor gives; and (6) draw a bar chart programme. Each member leads one document and checks another member's document. At the end, the group presents its job pack to the assessor, with every member speaking about the part they led. Nothing is opened or connected. Photograph each stage and hand in the job pack.
materials: Access to a training room or bay, with the supply isolated by the assessor
Drawing of the area and cable data sheet, from the assessor
Supplier lead times and a price list, from the assessor
Tape measure, laser measure, cable and pipe detector
Survey form, risk assessment and method statement forms, materials schedule form
Graph paper or a computer for the bar chart
Calculator, scale rule, pencils and coloured pens
photos: The group surveying the area and the board, with the survey form
The marked-up drawing with the new routes and boxes
The design current and voltage drop working
The signed risk assessment and method statement
The materials schedule with order dates
The group presenting the job pack
checklist: Took part in the survey and recorded findings accurately, without opening anything
Led one document and made it complete and correct
Worked out the current and the voltage drop correctly and drew the right conclusion
Included full safe isolation (lock, tag, prove dead with a tester checked before and after) in the method statement
Set realistic order dates from the lead times
Checked another member's document and noted corrections
Explained their part clearly in the presentation
safety: Do not open any board, box or accessory; the survey is visual only
Use the detector before marking any drill position, but do not drill
Use steps or ladders only as the Centre's rules allow, with someone footing them
Keep the area tidy and leave it as you found it

practical2.title: Team lock-off, setting out and materials readiness for a conduit job
practical2.brief: Part A, team isolation: on the Centre's isolation training board (not connected to any supply), the group acts as a team of electricians starting work on one circuit. One member, as team leader, completes an isolation record; every member fits their own lock to a multi-lock hasp and the leader fits a danger tag. The leader proves the tester on the proving unit, tests at the point of work between all conductors, and proves the tester again, while the others check each step against the method statement. Then the group shows the correct order for removing locks at the end of work. Each member takes a turn as leader. Part B, setting out: on a training bay or room, set out the routes and box positions for the job drawing from a datum at the finished floor level, using a laser level, after scanning with a detector. Part C, materials: check a delivery from the store against the materials schedule, record any shortages or damaged items on a form, and set up a tidy, labelled storage area. Check the test instruments for calibration dates and record them. Photograph each stage and hand in the isolation records and forms.
materials: Isolation training board (not connected to any supply)
Two-pole voltage tester and proving unit
Multi-lock hasp, a padlock for each member, danger tags
Isolation record forms and the method statement
Job drawing, laser level, tape measure, chalk line and detector
A delivery of conduit, fittings, boxes and cable from the store, with a materials schedule
Delivery check forms, labels and a marker
Test instruments with calibration labels, and a calibration log
photos: The hasp with every member's lock and the danger tag
The tester being proved on the proving unit before and after
The datum line and box positions set out with the laser level
The delivery check form with shortages noted
checklist: Fitted their own lock and explained why each worker uses their own
As leader, followed the full safe isolation order without missing a step
Tested between all conductors and proved the tester before and after
Removed locks in the right order and did not remove another member's lock
Set out box positions accurately from the finished floor datum
Checked delivered items carefully and recorded faults clearly
Checked and recorded calibration dates correctly
safety: The training board is never connected to a supply; treat it as live in your method all the same
Do not look into the laser beam
Lift drums and bundles of conduit safely, with help for heavy items
